newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Botha denies blame for Bisho slaying.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Botha denies blame for Bisho slaying.

text.p: South Africa's former foreign minister, Pik Botha, on Monday rejected African National Congress charges that the country's last white government was to blame for the 1992 "Bisho massacre" of 29 black protesters.

Botha told Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth Commission that former president F.W. de Klerk's government had tried to defuse the confrontation on the border between white South Africa and the then nominally independent black Ciskei homeland.
Twenty-nine demonstrators died and about 200 were wounded when homeland soldiers opened fire on ANC marchers demanding the dismissal of their ruler, Brigadier Oupa Gqozo.
ANC Secretary General Cyril Ramaphosa, who was amongst leaders of the march, said de Klerk's government was to blame for the killing because it was the real power behind Gqozo.
"The responsibility for the Bisho massacre rests squarely with the Ciskei regime and with the government of F.W. de Klerk, where the real power behind the Bisho government resided," Ramaphosa said.
Botha however said the regime was responsible for its own actions, adding: "Gqozo was not a puppet of the South African government."

Tutu's commission is devoting three days to testimony about the massacre, one of the bloodiest incidents of the four years between the legalisation of the ANC in 1990 and its victory in the country's first all-race elections in April 1994.
Recalling the incident, which rocked the democracy talks, Tutu said:
"It seemed as if we were entering a horrid night and the hopes for a settlement seemed to have been dashed."
Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils, who led a charge from the Bisho stadium towards the purpose-built homeland capital about a kilometre away, also blamed de Klerk.
He said that while he had been determined to break through Ciskei police lines to the town, he had been surprised to find a gaping hole in the stadium fence.
Acknowledging "a tragic miscalculation", he said: "We did not imagine that Gqozo, as cruel and desperate as we regarded him to be, would dare react with such brutal force."
The shooting erupted when Kasrils led a shouting group through the gap and into the firing line of soldiers hidden behind a sand embankment.
"I emphatically reject this allegation...that I knowingly and wilfully led innocent people to their slaughter," he said.
Botha said there could only be real reconciliation when political parties broke the apartheid-era mould.
Responding to reporters' questions after the hearing, he said he expected a political realignment in South Africa within a few years, but denied that he was leading the initiative.
"I'm out of politics now. I'm prepared to act as an advisor and if things develop in such a way that I can a role I will do so, but I'm not behind it," he said.
The crowd, including several people crippled in the September 1992 shooting, applauded Botha at the end of his lengthy testimony.
Ramaphosa, now one of the country's most influential black businessmen, told the panel probing the human rights record of the last 30 years of white rule of the fear felt by marchers.

"I thought it lasted forever. There was terror and panic all around," he said. "The saddest part was to see fairly elderly women dropping to the floor and crawling, to see the terror written on the faces of the young people."
